title: Fallout shelter kit
summary: What to keep at your shelter spot so the group can shelter without going out “for as long as 2 weeks, and maybe longer (civil defence handbooks, 1968 and 1985, dated).”

items.text: Battery-powered or hand-crank radio, preferably a NOAA weather radio
items.note: Keeps working when other ways of getting news fail.

items.text: Extra batteries for the radio
Flashlights or battery lanterns, with extra batteries
Drinking water for at least 2 weeks, as on the Home water store list
items.note: At least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day. Keep it where you will shelter.

items.text: Sealed, non-perishable food for at least 2 weeks
Manual can opener
Medicines: prescription and non-prescription, for at least 2 weeks
items.note: Include medicines taken regularly or likely to be needed.

items.text: First aid kit
Baby supplies: formula, bottles, diapers and wipes, if you have a baby
Pet food and extra water, if you have pets
A spare change of clothes for each person
Trash bags or plastic bags for clothes taken off after being outside
items.note: Seal the clothes in, and keep the bag where no one will touch it.

items.text: Soap, for washing skin and hair after being outside
Wipes or clean cloths, for wiping skin and hair if you can’t wash
items.note: Not household cleaning wipes. Hand sanitizer does not protect against radioactive material.

items.text: Dust masks or cloths to cover your mouth and nose if you must go outside
items.note: They help cut how much radioactive material you breathe. Getting inside is still the best protection.

items.text: Sleeping bag or warm blanket for each person
Battery carbon monoxide alarms near where people sleep
items.note: Never burn anything in a sealed room. Winter heat supplies are on the Home heat kit list.

items.text: Toilet and sanitation supplies, as on the Sanitation kit list
Cell phone with chargers and a backup battery
items.note: Text messages may get through when calls don’t.

items.text: Family emergency plan written down: meeting place if you can’t meet at home, and an out-of-state contact
Books, games or other activities for children

sources.name: Ready.gov (FEMA), Radiation Emergencies (last updated June 14, 2024)
sources.used: Battery-powered or hand-crank radio that keeps working when other communication fails; spare change of clothes for each family member; trash bag for contaminated clothing; sealed food, water and medicine; family emergency communication plan, meeting place, out-of-state contact; soap and water, or a wipe or clean wet cloth; no household cleaning wipes on skin; hand sanitizer does not protect against radioactive material

sources.name: Ready.gov (FEMA), Build A Kit (ready.gov/kit; undated)
sources.used: Flashlight; extra batteries; first aid kit; dust mask to help filter contaminated air; manual can opener; cell phone with chargers and a backup battery; prescription and non-prescription medications; infant formula, bottles, diapers and wipes; pet food and extra water for your pet; sleeping bag or warm blanket for each person; books, games or activities for children; non-perishable food

sources.name: CDC, Frequently Asked Questions about Radiation Emergencies (last reviewed April 19, 2022; updated April 12, 2024)
sources.used: Radio, preferably a NOAA weather radio; extra batteries; bottled water and non-perishable foods; text messages when calls are hard; covering mouth and nose reduces the radioactive material you breathe

sources.name: CDC, Dirty Bombs: Frequently Asked Questions (last reviewed April 10, 2024)
sources.used: Seal removed clothing in a plastic bag and put it where others will not touch it

sources.name: CDC, Potassium Iodide (KI) (last reviewed April 16, 2024; updated January 30, 2025)
sources.used: Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned is always the best protection

sources.name: FEMA, Protection in the Nuclear Age (June 1985; dated civil defence publication)
sources.used: Two-week stock of water, food and supplies to bring to shelter; medicines taken regularly or likely to be needed; battery-powered radio and flashlight or lantern with spare batteries

sources.name: Living in a closed-up house, How much water you need and How long to stay in (other topics in this app)
sources.used: Flashlights or battery lanterns, not candles or fuel lanterns (CDC, CPSC); battery CO alarms near where people sleep (CDC, CPSC); never burn anything in a sealed room; 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day for 2 weeks; “for as long as 2 weeks, and maybe longer (civil defence handbooks, 1968 and 1985, dated)” with no word from anyone (How long to stay in)
